questions.q: Which gas makes up about 78 per cent of the Earth's atmosphere?
questions.a: nitrogen

questions.q: Besides its many gases, which two other things does the chapter say the atmosphere contains?
questions.a: water vapour and tiny dust particles
o: water vapour and tiny dust particles

questions.q: Read the statements about the composition of the atmosphere. Statement I: Krypton, xenon and hydrogen are among the gases found in the atmosphere in lesser quantities. Statement II: The atmosphere holds a larger share of carbon dioxide than of argon. Statement III: The composition of the atmosphere varies with altitude. Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I and III only

questions.q: Assertion (A): The atmosphere stays wrapped around the Earth like a blanket instead of drifting away into space. Reason (R): The atmosphere is pulled down around the Earth by gravity. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: True or False: Ozone is one of the gases present in the atmosphere, but only in lesser quantities.
questions.a: True. The chapter lists ozone with carbon dioxide, argon, helium, neon, krypton, xenon and hydrogen as gases found in lesser quantities; nitrogen and oxygen are the most abundant.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: ozone is named among the gases in lesser quantities, while nitrogen and oxygen are the most abundant

questions.q: (a) What is the atmosphere? (b) Give one thing you notice when you look up at the sky that the chapter says is a result of the atmosphere.
questions.a: (a) The atmosphere is the blanket of air surrounding the Earth, a mixture of gases held around the Earth by gravity. (b) Any one: floating clouds, sunshine or a breeze.
s: (a) A blanket of air (mixture of gases) surrounding the Earth
(b) One example: clouds, sunshine or a breeze

questions.q: The chapter's pie chart shows argon at 0.93% and carbon dioxide at 0.04% of the air. (a) About how many times as much argon as carbon dioxide is there? (b) The chapter adds that water vapour, not shown in the pie chart, generally ranges from 0.1 per cent to 0.4 per cent of the air. Even at its lowest, how many times the carbon dioxide share is the water vapour share?
questions.a: (a) 0.93 / 0.04 = 23.25, so about 23 times as much argon as carbon dioxide. (b) 0.1 / 0.04 = 2.5, so even at its lowest the water vapour share is 2.5 times the carbon dioxide share (and at 0.4 per cent it is 10 times).
s: (a) 0.93 / 0.04 = about 23 times

questions.q: Answer each part in one line. (a) Which gas is the second most abundant in the atmosphere? (b) Between what limits does the amount of water vapour in the air generally range? (c) What does the chapter say about the composition of the atmosphere as you go higher?
questions.a: (a) Oxygen (21%). (b) Generally from 0.1 per cent to 0.4 per cent. (c) The composition of the atmosphere varies with altitude.
s: (a) Oxygen
(b) 0.1 to 0.4 per cent
(c) It varies with altitude

questions.q: The chapter says the atmosphere influences temperature, humidity and air pressure. For each of these three, name the feature of the atmosphere, described in the chapter, that explains the link.
questions.a: Temperature: the atmosphere traps some of the Sun's energy and stops it escaping back into space, so it regulates the Earth's temperature. Humidity: the atmosphere holds water vapour, and water vapour in the air is what humidity is. Air pressure: the air has weight, and the pressure exerted by the weight of air on the Earth's surface is air pressure.
s: Temperature: trapping some of the Sun's energy so it does not escape to space
Humidity: the water vapour the atmosphere holds
Air pressure: the weight of the air pressing on the Earth's surface

questions.q: Answer each part in one line. (a) Name the harmful radiation from the Sun that the chapter says the atmosphere shields us from. (b) How does the atmosphere regulate the Earth's temperature? (c) Nitrogen is 78% and oxygen 21% of the air. By how many percentage points does nitrogen exceed oxygen? (d) Name any two gases, other than carbon dioxide and argon, that are present in lesser quantities. (e) In which two processes does water vapour play a significant role?
questions.a: (a) Ultraviolet radiation. (b) It traps some of the Sun's energy and prevents it from escaping back into space. (c) 78 - 21 = 57 percentage points. (d) Any two of helium, neon, krypton, xenon, ozone, hydrogen. (e) Cloud formation and precipitation.
s: (a) Ultraviolet radiation
(b) Traps some of the Sun's energy so it does not escape to space
(d) Two of helium, neon, krypton, xenon, ozone, hydrogen
(e) Cloud formation and precipitation

questions.q: What is the name of the transition zone that separates the troposphere from the stratosphere?
questions.a: the tropopause

questions.q: A probe rising straight up radios two clues from one height: the air around it is very thin, and light gases such as helium and hydrogen are drifting away from there into space. Using the chapter's layer heights, at about what height is the probe?
questions.a: Above 700 km, in the exosphere, the layer above the thermosphere (80-700 km).
o: Above 700 km, in the exosphere, the layer above the thermosphere (80-700 km).
Between 80 and 700 km, in the thermosphere.
Between 50 and 80 km, in the mesosphere.
Between 12 and 50 km, in the stratosphere.

questions.q: Match each term in Column I with what the chapter says about it in Column II. Column I: 1. Tropopause  2. Stratopause  3. Ionosphere  4. Aurora Australis. Column II: (a) the boundary between the stratosphere and the mesosphere  (b) the transition zone between the troposphere and the stratosphere  (c) a part of the thermosphere  (d) the coloured lights seen in the Southern Hemisphere
Assertion (A): Most meteorites entering from space burn up in the mesosphere. Reason (R): In the mesosphere, temperature decreases with increasing altitude. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: (a) What does the word 'aurora' mean in Latin? (b) Why does an aurora show different colours?
questions.a: (a) 'Dawn' or 'morning light'. (b) Charged particles from the Sun (the solar wind) interact with different gases in the atmosphere, and each gas glows with a particular colour.
s: (a) Dawn or morning light
(b) Solar-wind particles meet different gases and each gas glows with its own colour

questions.q: True or False: The troposphere holds the air we breathe, but most of the water vapour and clouds are found higher up, in the stratosphere.
questions.a: False. The troposphere holds the air we breathe along with most of the water vapour and clouds; the stratosphere is free of clouds and weather disturbances.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: most water vapour and clouds are in the troposphere; the stratosphere is free of clouds

questions.q: Answer each part in one line. (a) In which layer of the atmosphere do the auroras occur? (b) Which layer contains the layer of ozone gas? (c) Name the uppermost layer of the atmosphere and say what its air is like.
questions.a: (a) The thermosphere. (b) The stratosphere. (c) The exosphere, where the air is very thin.
s: (a) Thermosphere
(b) Stratosphere
(c) Exosphere, with very thin air

questions.q: Rehan says, 'The thermosphere is only a thin band at the top of the atmosphere, much thinner than the layers below it.' Use the chapter's heights (the mesosphere reaches up to 80 km; the thermosphere extends from 80 to 700 km) to test his claim.
questions.a: The thermosphere is 700 - 80 = 620 km thick. The troposphere, stratosphere and mesosphere together reach only up to 80 km, so all three lower layers together are 80 km thick. 620 / 80 = 7.75, so the thermosphere alone is nearly eight times as thick as the three lower layers together; Rehan's claim is wrong.
s: Thickness of the thermosphere: 700 - 80 = 620 km
The three lower layers together: up to 80 km; 620 / 80 = 7.75 times
Verdict: the claim is wrong; the thermosphere is far thicker

questions.q: Four students write labels for a classroom chart of the layers of the atmosphere. Label 1: 'Temperature falls with height in every layer.' Label 2: 'Radio waves sent up from the Earth are reflected back by the thermosphere, of which the ionosphere is a part.' Label 3: 'Aeroplanes fly in the stratosphere because it contains the ozone layer.' Label 4: 'The exosphere has thick air rich in oxygen.' Judge each label as correct or wrong and correct any that are wrong.
questions.a: Label 1 is wrong: temperature decreases with altitude only in the troposphere and the mesosphere; it rises rapidly in the thermosphere. Label 2 is correct: the thermosphere reflects radio waves back to the Earth and the ionosphere is part of it. Label 3 gives the wrong reason: the stratosphere is ideal for aeroplanes because it is free of clouds and weather disturbances; the ozone layer is a separate feature that filters harmful radiation. Label 4 is wrong: the exosphere has very thin air, and light gases like helium and hydrogen float into space from it.
s: Label 1 wrong: temperature falls with height only in the troposphere and mesosphere
Label 2 correct: the thermosphere (with the ionosphere) reflects radio waves
Label 3 wrong reason: aeroplanes use the stratosphere because it is free of clouds and weather disturbances
Label 4 wrong: exosphere air is very thin; light gases escape from it

questions.q: A research probe rises straight up and sends readings at five heights: 5 km, 30 km, 60 km, 300 km and 750 km. For each height, name the layer of the atmosphere the probe is in and give one feature of that layer from the chapter, saying also whether the temperature there is falling or rising with height where the chapter tells you.
questions.a: 5 km: troposphere (up to about 12 km); weather such as rain, fog and hail; temperature falls with height. 30 km: stratosphere (up to 50 km); ozone layer, free of clouds. 60 km: mesosphere (up to 80 km); most meteorites burn up here; temperature falls with height. 300 km: thermosphere (80-700 km); temperature rises very rapidly; radio waves reflected, auroras occur. 750 km: exosphere, above 700 km; very thin air, helium and hydrogen float into space.
s: 5 km: troposphere; weather occurs, temperature falls with height
30 km: stratosphere; ozone layer, free of clouds
60 km: mesosphere; meteorites burn up, temperature falls with height
300 km: thermosphere; temperature rises rapidly, radio waves reflected or auroras
750 km: exosphere; very thin air, light gases escape to space

questions.q: In the chapter's figure of the temperature zones of the Earth, what is the zone between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn, where sunlight strikes most directly, called?
questions.a: the Torrid Zone

questions.q: On a walk, Neha feels the wind on her face, hears the leaves rustle and sees an ordinary wind vane turning. Using the chapter's table of wind speeds, which category is this wind?
questions.a: Light breeze, 6-11 km/hr

questions.q: Place X lies near 10 degrees N and Place Y near 70 degrees N. Using the chapter's ideas of insolation and temperature zones, which comparison is correct?
questions.a: X gets more insolation because sunlight strikes it more directly, so X is generally warmer; Y lies in the Frigid Zone.
o: X gets more insolation because sunlight strikes it more directly, so X is generally warmer; Y lies in the Frigid Zone.
Y gets more insolation because it is nearer the pole, so Y is generally warmer; X lies in the Temperate Zone.
Both get the same insolation because the Sun shines on the whole Earth; only their winds differ.
X gets less insolation because sunlight there comes at a low angle; Y lies in the Torrid Zone.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The sea breeze blows from the sea to the land during the day. Reason (R): In the afternoon the sea becomes warmer than the land, so a low-pressure region forms over the sea. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: (a) What is precipitation, according to the chapter? (b) Name two forms of precipitation other than rain.
questions.a: (a) When a part of the atmosphere becomes saturated with water vapour, the vapour condenses and falls on the Earth due to gravity; this is precipitation. (b) Any two of drizzle, snow, sleet and hail.
s: (a) Saturated air: water vapour condenses and falls to the Earth due to gravity
(b) Two of drizzle, snow, sleet, hail

questions.q: The chapter's figure of temperature zones marks the Tropic of Cancer at 23½ degrees N and the Arctic Circle at 66½ degrees N. (a) In which zone does a city at 50 degrees N lie? (b) Compared with a city at 5 degrees N, will it receive more or less insolation, and why?
questions.a: (a) The North Temperate Zone, since 50 degrees N lies between 23½ degrees N and 66½ degrees N. (b) Less insolation, because insolation decreases from the equator towards the poles; at 5 degrees N, near the equator, sunlight strikes more directly.
s: (a) North Temperate Zone (between 23½ and 66½ degrees N)
(b) Less insolation, because insolation decreases from the equator towards the poles

questions.q: Answer each part in one line. (a) What is insolation? (b) How does the amount of insolation change from the equator towards the poles? (c) What happens to temperature as a result?
questions.a: (a) The incoming solar energy from the Sun that is intercepted by the Earth. (b) It decreases from the equator towards the poles. (c) Temperature also decreases from the equator towards the poles.
s: (a) Incoming solar energy intercepted by the Earth
(b) It decreases from the equator towards the poles
(c) Temperature decreases from the equator towards the poles

questions.q: A village in a dry region has had very little rain for many years in a row. Using the chapter's account of precipitation, explain three linked effects this long absence of rainfall has on the village.
questions.a: First, a long absence of rainfall results in a dry climate. Second, since most groundwater is collected from rainwater, the village's groundwater is not refilled and wells can run low. Third, because rain lowers the temperature of a place, without rain the village does not get that cooling.
s: A long absence of rainfall gives a dry climate
Groundwater is not refilled, since most groundwater comes from rainwater
No cooling from rain, since rain lowers the temperature of a place

questions.q: A kite-flying club on a sea coast keeps a temperature log for one summer day. At 2 p.m. the beach sand (land) is at 34 degrees C and the sea water at 28 degrees C. At 2 a.m. the land is at 22 degrees C and the sea at 26 degrees C. The club flies kites only when the wind blows from the sea towards the land, so that kites drift over the beach and not out over the water. (a) Which local wind blows at 2 p.m., and in which direction? (b) Which local wind blows at 2 a.m., and in which direction? (c) Using the temperature differences, which of the two winds is likely to be the gentler one, and why? (d) At which of the two times should the club fly its kites?
questions.a: (a) The sea breeze, from the sea to the land, because the land is warmer (34 degrees C against 28 degrees C) and low pressure forms over the land. (b) The land breeze, from the land to the sea, because the land has cooled faster than the sea (22 degrees C against 26 degrees C). (c) The land breeze: the difference at night is 26 - 22 = 4 degrees C, against 34 - 28 = 6 degrees C by day; the chapter says that at night the difference in temperature and pressure is low, so the wind speed is low. (d) At 2 p.m., when the sea breeze blows from the sea towards the land.
s: (a) Sea breeze, sea to land, as the land is warmer
(b) Land breeze, land to sea, as the land has cooled faster
(c) Land breeze is gentler: 4 degrees C difference against 6, so lower pressure difference and lower speed
(d) At 2 p.m., when the sea breeze blows towards the land

questions.q: A student's weather diary has four entries. Entry 1: 'This July was the wettest of the last three years, so our town's climate has changed.' Entry 2: 'Pressure over our town is low today, so I expect clear and sunny skies.' Entry 3: 'The wind reached our town from the cooler hills, where the pressure was higher.' Entry 4: 'Today it sleeted; sleet is a form of precipitation.' Judge each entry as correct or wrong, giving the chapter's reason.
questions.a: Entry 1 is wrong: climate is the sum of weather conditions over a long period, usually thirty years or more; three years of July rain describe weather, not a change of climate. Entry 2 is wrong: low pressure is associated with cloudy skies and wet weather; clear and sunny skies go with high pressure. Entry 3 is correct: cold air is heavy and sinks, giving high pressure, and air always moves from high-pressure to low-pressure areas. Entry 4 is correct: precipitation includes drizzle, rain, snow, sleet and hail.
s: Entry 1 wrong: climate needs about thirty years or more of weather
Entry 2 wrong: low pressure brings cloudy, wet weather; clear skies go with high pressure
Entry 3 correct: air moves from high pressure (cool hills) to low pressure
Entry 4 correct: sleet is one of the forms of precipitation

questions.q: How does the chapter broadly classify the climate of India?
questions.a: tropical monsoon

questions.q: On what are India's six traditional seasons based, according to the chapter?
questions.a: the astronomical division of the 12 months into six parts
o: the astronomical division of the 12 months into six parts
the IMD's records of temperature and rainfall
the arrival and retreat of the south-west monsoon
the hottest and coldest months of each region

questions.q: Read the statements about the seasons of India recognised by the IMD. Statement I: The winter season generally lasts from December to early April. Statement II: The summer or pre-monsoon season may last up to July in north-western India. Statement III: The post-monsoon season lasts from October to February. Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I and II only

questions.q: Match each traditional Indian season (Ṛtu) in Column I with its Gregorian months in Column II, as given in the chapter's Table 3.2. Column I: 1. Vasanta  2. Grīṣhma  3. Śharad  4. Śhiśhira. Column II: (a) January-February  (b) March-April  (c) September-October  (d) May-June
(a) Which are the coldest months of the year in India, according to the chapter? (b) What is the other name the chapter gives to the summer season?
questions.a: (a) December and January. (b) The pre-monsoon season.
s: (a) December and January
(b) Pre-monsoon

questions.q: True or False: The traditional Indian seasons have exactly the same months and the same length in every part of the country.
questions.a: False. The chapter's note to Table 3.2 says that these seasons and their duration may vary across different parts of the country.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: the seasons and their duration may vary across different parts of the country

questions.q: The chapter explains how the year is divided into seasons. (a) On what kind of conditions is this division based? (b) Give two of the pairs of contrasting conditions the chapter lists. (c) Why does a single unusual day not change the season?
questions.a: (a) On generalised monthly atmospheric conditions, a common pattern over a few weeks or months. (b) Any two of: cool or hot, windy or calm, cloudy or bright, wet or dry. (c) Weather can fluctuate even within a single day, but a season is decided by the common pattern over weeks or months, not by one day.
s: (a) Generalised monthly conditions, a pattern over weeks or months
(b) Two of cool/hot, windy/calm, cloudy/bright, wet/dry
(c) Daily weather fluctuates; a season follows the pattern over weeks or months

questions.q: A school in north India is preparing a season calendar based on the four seasons recognised by the Indian Meteorological Department. Using the months the chapter gives for each season, write the IMD season for each of these dates: (a) 15 January (b) 20 May (c) 10 August (d) 20 November.
questions.a: (a) 15 January: winter (December to early April). (b) 20 May: summer or pre-monsoon (April to June). (c) 10 August: monsoon or rainy season (June to September). (d) 20 November: post-monsoon or retreating monsoon (October to December).
s: (a) Winter
(b) Summer or pre-monsoon
(c) Monsoon or rainy season
(d) Post-monsoon (retreating monsoon)

questions.q: Using the chapter's Table 3.2 and its account of the four IMD seasons, take each of these five traditional seasons in turn: Vasanta, Grīṣhma, Varṣhā, Śharad and Hemanta. For each, give its Gregorian months and the IMD season or seasons into which those months fall.
questions.a: Vasanta: March-April; winter (to early April) and the start of summer (from April). Grīṣhma: May-June; summer or pre-monsoon. Varṣhā: July-August; monsoon. Śharad: September-October; the end of the monsoon (September) and the start of post-monsoon (October). Hemanta: November-December; post-monsoon, with December also the start of winter.
s: Vasanta: March-April; winter into summer
Grīṣhma: May-June; summer or pre-monsoon
Varṣhā: July-August; monsoon
Śharad: September-October; monsoon into post-monsoon
Hemanta: November-December; post-monsoon, December also winter

questions.q: A sports board will hold two outdoor athletics meets in the same year. Meet 1 is in a city in northern India and Meet 2 is in a city in southern India. Each meet must be held in either late April or late May, and the board would like to save money by holding both in the same month. The board's doctors advise against holding a meet in the month that is the hottest of the year in that region. (a) Which month is the hottest in northern regions, and which in western and southern regions? (b) In which IMD season do late April and late May fall, and what average temperature does the chapter give across most of inland India in that season? (c) Can the board hold both meets in the same month and still follow the doctors' advice? Explain. (d) Which month should each meet use?
questions.a: (a) May in northern regions; April in western and southern regions. (b) The summer or pre-monsoon season (April to June); the average temperature across most of inland India ranges from 32-40 degrees C. (c) No: late April is the hottest month in the south, so it rules out Meet 2, and late May is the hottest month in the north, so it rules out Meet 1; neither month suits both cities. (d) Meet 1 (north) in late April and Meet 2 (south) in late May.
s: (a) May in the north; April in the west and south
(b) Summer or pre-monsoon; 32-40 degrees C
(c) No single month works: April is hottest in the south, May in the north
(d) Meet 1 in late April, Meet 2 in late May

questions.q: Which statement about the south-west monsoon is correct, according to the chapter?
questions.a: It accounts for most of the rainfall in the country throughout the year.
o: It accounts for most of the rainfall in the country throughout the year.
It blows from the land to the sea between October and February.
It brings cold and dry winds to most parts of India.
It is caused by the land cooling faster than the sea.

questions.q: Under the National Monsoon Mission, which ministry of the Government of India has developed state-of-the-art weather and climate prediction models?
questions.a: the Ministry of Earth Sciences

questions.q: Match each term in Column I with the description in Column II, as given in the chapter. Column I: 1. South-west monsoon  2. North-east monsoon  3. Monsoon  4. National Monsoon Mission. Column II: (a) cold and dry winds from land to sea, from October to February  (b) moist winds from sea to land, from June to September  (c) the seasonal reversal in the wind direction during a year  (d) aims to enhance monsoon predictions for India over all time frames

Assertion (A): During summer, a low-pressure area forms over the Indian subcontinent. Reason (R): During summer, the landmass of India heats up faster than the surrounding oceans. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: (a) Why are monsoon winds called seasonal winds? (b) Name the two kinds of monsoon the chapter describes.
questions.a: (a) Because their direction reverses with the season during a year. (b) The south-west (summer) monsoon and the north-east (winter) monsoon.
s: (a) Their direction reverses with the season
(b) South-west (summer) and north-east (winter) monsoon

questions.q: (a) Who wrote Meghadūtam, and around when was it written? (b) Name the two things about the monsoon that it records.
questions.a: (a) Kālidāsa, around the 5th century CE. (b) The date of the onset of the monsoon over central India, and the path of the monsoon clouds.
s: (a) Kālidāsa, around the 5th century CE
(b) Onset date over central India and the path of monsoon clouds

questions.q: The chapter's map of normal dates of the advancing south-west monsoon runs from 22 May to 8 July. Its map of the retreating monsoon runs from 17 September to 15 October. (i) How many days does the monsoon normally take to advance over the country? (ii) How many days does it take to retreat? (iii) Which happens faster, and by how many days?
questions.a: (i) 22 May to 8 July: 9 days left in May + 30 in June + 8 in July = 47 days. (ii) 17 September to 15 October: 13 days left in September + 15 in October = 28 days. (iii) The retreat is faster, by 47 - 28 = 19 days.
s: (i) Advance: 47 days
(ii) Retreat: 28 days
(iii) The retreat is faster, by 19 days

questions.q: In a school debate, Kunal argues: 'Now that the National Monsoon Mission has state-of-the-art prediction models, the old Indian methods of forecasting rain are of no use to anyone.' Evaluate his claim. In your answer: (a) say why Indians first worked out ways to predict rainfall; (b) state what Kṛiṣhiparāśhara's and Varāhamihira's methods were based on; (c) say what the chapter tells us about these methods today; (d) state what the National Monsoon Mission and Mission Mausam aim to do; (e) give your verdict on Kunal's claim.
questions.a: (a) Crop production often depended on seasonal monsoon rains, so Indians worked out methods to predict rainfall. (b) Kṛiṣhiparāśhara's main technique used the positions of the Moon and the Sun; Varāhamihira's Bṛihatsaṁhitā used the lunar mansions (nakṣhatras). (c) Even today a large number of farming practices in India are based on these ancient methods. (d) The National Monsoon Mission aims to enhance monsoon predictions for India over all time frames; Mission Mausam aims to make India 'Weather Ready' and 'Climate Smart' with timely, precise forecasts for agriculture, disaster management and rural development. (e) Kunal is wrong to say the old methods are of no use to anyone: many farming practices still follow them, even though modern missions improve forecasts; the two exist side by side.
s: (a) Crops depended on monsoon rains, so rainfall had to be predicted
(b) Moon and Sun positions (Kṛiṣhiparāśhara); lunar mansions (Varāhamihira)
(c) Many farming practices today are still based on these methods
(d) NMM: better monsoon predictions over all time frames; Mission Mausam: Weather Ready, Climate Smart
(e) Verdict: the claim is wrong, as old methods are still used alongside modern models

questions.q: A school weather club compares two months on India's south-east coast. In June, the land near the coast measures 38 degrees C while the nearby sea measures 29 degrees C. In December, the land measures 20 degrees C while the sea measures 26 degrees C. The club also notes that most of north and central India is dry in December, yet coastal Tamil Nadu gets heavy rain. (a) In June, over which surface does low pressure form, which way do the winds blow, and which monsoon is this? (b) In December, over which surface does high pressure form, which way do the winds blow, and which monsoon is this? (c) Why do the December winds, which are dry over the land, bring rain to coastal Tamil Nadu? (d) Which of the two monsoons gives most of India's rainfall in a year?
questions.a: (a) Low pressure forms over the land, which is warmer (38 against 29 degrees C); moist winds blow from the sea to the land: the south-west (summer) monsoon. (b) High pressure forms over the land, which has cooled faster (20 against 26 degrees C); cold dry winds blow from the land to the sea: the north-east (winter) monsoon. (c) The north-east winds pick up moisture as they pass over the Bay of Bengal and bring rain to the eastern coast, especially Tamil Nadu. (d) The south-west monsoon, which accounts for most of the rainfall in the country throughout the year.
s: (a) Low pressure over the warmer land; sea-to-land moist winds; south-west monsoon
(b) High pressure over the cooler land; land-to-sea dry winds; north-east monsoon
(c) The winds pick up moisture over the Bay of Bengal and rain on the east coast
(d) The south-west monsoon gives most of the rainfall

questions.q: Four students write one line each for a class quiz on the monsoon. Asha: 'The monsoon was first noticed only recently, with weather satellites.' Bilal: 'The word monsoon comes from the Arabic word mausim, meaning rain.' Chitra: 'The monsoon affects transport, festivals and employment, especially in rural areas.' Dev: 'A weak monsoon is dangerous because it causes floods.' Judge each line as correct or wrong and correct the wrong ones using the chapter.
questions.a: Asha is wrong: sailors who came to India in ancient times were among the first to notice the monsoon, and Arab traders gave it its name. Bilal is wrong in part: monsoon does come from the Arabic mausim, but mausim means 'season', not rain. Chitra is correct: the chapter says the monsoon affects daily life, transport, festivals and employment, especially in rural areas. Dev is wrong: excessive rainfall causes floods, while weak monsoons can lead to droughts.
s: Asha wrong: ancient sailors were among the first to notice the monsoon
Bilal wrong: mausim means season, not rain
Chitra correct: transport, festivals and employment are affected

questions.q: A newspaper column claims: 'Climate change is caused entirely by human beings, but the harm falls only on forests, glaciers and wild animals.' The claim has two halves. questions.q: Two villages lie on the banks of the same river in Punjab during the heavy monsoon of 2025. In Village A, houses and farms stand within 50 m of the river, the old earthen embankment (dhūsī bāndh) was last repaired thirty years ago, and the flood warning reached people only two hours before the water arrived. In Village B, houses stand 600 m from the river, the embankment was strengthened recently, and the warning reached people a full day earlier. Both villages received the same heavy rain. (a) Name two natural causes that affected both villages. (b) List the human-made causes from the chapter that are present in Village A. (c) Explain why Village B is likely to suffer less damage. (d) Suggest two steps Village A should take before the next monsoon, linking each to a cause.
questions.a: (a) Any two: very heavy monsoon rain; western disturbances bringing more moisture and rain; rivers already flowing high; rain in the hills (Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir) adding water. (b) Building houses and farms too close to the river; weak and old embankments; a late flood warning. (c) Village B leaves more natural space for floodwater to spread, has a stronger embankment to hold back rising water, and its people had a day to prepare. (d) For example: strengthen or rebuild the old embankment (weak embankments), and set up an early, clear flood warning (late warnings); moving new building back from the river (building too close) is another sound step.
s: (a) Two natural causes: heavy monsoon rain, western disturbances, rivers already high, rain in the hills
(b) Village A: building too close to the river, weak old embankment, late warning
(c) Village B: more space for floodwater, stronger embankment, earlier warning
(d) Two steps for Village A, each linked to a human-made cause
